name: Innate lymphoid cells (ILC1, ILC2 and ILC3)
markers: No CD3 and no antigen receptor (they carry no rearranged T-cell or B-cell receptor)
ILC2: GATA3 (transcription factor), ST2 (the IL-33 receptor), CRTH2 (human marker)
ILC3: RORγt (transcription factor); NKp44 (human marker; only some ILC3)
summary: Lymphocytes of the innate immune system that carry no antigen receptor, so they respond to alarm signals from damaged tissue, not to one antigen. Three groups mirror the T helper cells: ILC1 make IFN-γ, ILC2 make IL-5 and IL-13, ILC3 make IL-17 and IL-22. Most stay in one tissue and are rare in blood.
functions: Develop from lymphoid progenitors, the same family that gives T and B cells, but never rearrange antigen receptor genes, so they cannot recognise one specific antigen. They read cytokines and alarm signals from epithelial and other tissue cells, and sit mostly at barrier surfaces such as gut, lung and skin. Here group 1 means ILC1; NK cells, the cytotoxic group 1 cells, have their own profile.
Group 1 (ILC1): depend on the transcription factor T-bet and make IFN-γ and TNF when IL-12, IL-15 and IL-18 arrive. They help defend against viruses and microbes that live inside cells.

Group 2 (ILC2): epithelial cells release the alarmins IL-25, IL-33 and TSLP after damage or worm invasion, and ILC2 (GATA3-dependent) answer within hours by making IL-5, IL-13 and amphiregulin, a growth factor that helps tissue repair. In mice they are an early source of IL-13 in worm infection.

Group 3 (ILC3): depend on the transcription factor RORγt. IL-23 and IL-1β, made by dendritic cells and macrophages, make them release IL-22, which acts on epithelial cells, and IL-17, which brings in neutrophils. In mice, IL-17-making innate lymphoid cells, not Th17 cells, controlled Candida infection of the mouth. A related cell, the lymphoid tissue inducer, builds lymph nodes in the embryo (mouse evidence).

Keeps eosinophils and some macrophages going. In mice, ILC2 make IL-5 constantly, which keeps blood IL-5 and eosinophil numbers up; in fat tissue their IL-5 and IL-13 sustain eosinophils and alternatively activated macrophages.

In human skin: healthy skin holds mainly ILC2 and ILC3 lacking NKp44, with few ILC1. ILC2 are enriched in the lesions of atopic dermatitis, and NKp44-positive ILC3 rise in psoriasis. Circulating human ILC carry the skin-homing marker CLA.

In mouse skin: dermal ILC2 constantly make IL-13, sit beside mast cells and, in that work, suppressed them. IL-17 and IL-22 from skin-invading RORγt-positive innate lymphocytes (and γδ T cells), not Th17 cells, drove psoriasis-like inflammation.

Mostly stay put. In adult mice ILCs are kept up and expanded locally, with little exchange through blood. Exceptions exist: IL-25- or worm-activated ILC2 leave the gut through lymph and blood, guided by S1P, and reach the lung; and lymphoid-tissue-inducer-like ILC3 travel from gut to draining lymph nodes using CCR7 (mouse evidence). Human blood carries ILC precursors that can make all ILC types and seed tissues.

Talks to T cells. In mice, ILC2 carry MHC class II and present antigen to CD4 T cells, and T-cell IL-2 drives ILC2 growth and IL-13 production, a two-way exchange that supports Th2 responses and worm expulsion. RORγt-positive ILC3 limit CD4 T-cell responses to gut bacteria.

Debated: how fixed the three groups are. In culture and in some tissues, ILCs convert between groups: human ILC3 and ILC1 into each other (IL-12, IL-23, IL-1β), and ILC2 into ILC1-like cells (IL-1β, IL-12).

Debated: how much ILCs matter in healthy people. In people with severe combined immunodeficiency treated by stem cell transplants, ILCs stayed low for decades with no particular susceptibility to disease, which suggests T cells can cover for them. Others dispute whether this shows redundancy.
abundance: Very rare in blood. More numerous at barrier surfaces such as the gut lining, lungs and skin, though still outnumbered there by T cells. Counts and the mix of groups differ by tissue, species and disease.
